notes: Planning JR on silage clamp GPDO classification; Sage holistic approach and quashing order are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Dennis v Sevenoaks: silage clamp permitted development and holistic planning control

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Neighbours challenged Sevenoaks' decision that sleeper walls for a silage clamp at Hilders Farm were permitted development not requiring prior notification under the 1995 GPDO.
The council treated the concrete base and retaining walls as separate schemes, relying on a mistaken belief that the floor reused a demolished barn base.
Mr Vicary had sought prior approval for a silage pit in July 2001 and concreted the base shortly after the council required prior approval for siting and design.
The walls' primary function was to retain silage within an above-ground pit rather than to enclose land as a means of enclosure under Part 2 Class A.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a local planning authority decision on permitted development and prior notification under the GPDO.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; the council's decision quashed and permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Planning control requires a holistic view of the totality of operations originally intended; a decision-maker who fails to consider the whole silage clamp scheme and relies on an irrelevant mistaken fact acts unlawfully, and walls whose primary purpose is silage retention may fall within Part 6 as part of a building rather than Part 2 as a means of enclosure.
legal_issues: Whether the silage clamp should be treated as one scheme or disassembled into separate permitted components
Whether the council had regard to Mr Vicary's original intended operations from July 2001
Whether the proposed walls were a means of enclosure under Part 2 Class A or part of a building under Part 6
Whether Prengate supports a mechanistic dual-function approach to enclosure walls
linked_authorities: Sage v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions [2003] UKHL 22
Prengate Properties Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1973] 25 P&CR 311

notes: PACE production order and legal professional privilege; Cox and Railton and Francis principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Hallinan: PACE production order and privilege where conspiracy to pervert justice alleged
key_facts: Patel's solicitors resisted a Crown Court production order for material relating to witness Mary King in a cocaine supply trial.
Police had freestanding evidence that King and a chambers clerk conspired to pervert the course of justice by preparing a false account of Patel's arrest.
The circuit judge found reasonable grounds that the material was held with intention of furthering a criminal purpose and was not privileged.
The solicitors were innocent of wrongdoing but held prima facie privileged documents converted from King's draft into section 9 witness statements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a Crown Court production order under PACE 1984 Schedule 1.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the judge was entitled to conclude privilege did not attach and the production order stood.
enrichment.ratio: Items held with the intention of furthering a criminal purpose are not subject to legal professional privilege under section 10(2); where there is freestanding independent evidence of a continuing conspiracy to pervert justice, the court may determine privilege without first resolving trial issues such as alibi or perjury.
legal_issues: Whether section 10(2) PACE excluded privilege for communications connected with the defendants' case
Whether the judge erred by treating the conspiracy as already complete rather than continuing
Whether analysis of trial issues was required before privilege could be defeated
Whether Article 6 rights prevented disclosure of defence-related material
linked_authorities: R v Cox and Railton (1884) 14 QBD 153
R v Central Criminal Court, ex parte Francis and Francis [1989] 1 AC 346
R v Snaresbrook Crown Court, ex parte DPP [1988] QB 532

notes: CFA success fee appeal case management; Brooke LJ's directions on rehearing and costs conditions are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Ungi v Liverpool: CFA success fee appeal and abuse of process application
key_facts: A child tripped on a council-owned grass verge; a 100 per cent CFA success fee was agreed and judgment entered after limited admissions.
On detailed assessment the district judge apportioned success fee by risk stages; the circuit judge held the full 100 per cent fee applied to assessment costs.
The defendant sought permission to appeal and the claimant applied to set aside permission on abuse-of-process grounds because new arguments were raised.
The defendant wished to argue for the first time that a lower success fee of about 66.6 per cent would have been reasonable at the outset.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal case-management hearing on an application to set aside permission to appeal in CFA success fee detailed assessment proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application to set aside permission refused with costs; appeal to continue subject to conditions preserving below costs and limiting Court of Appeal costs, with a re-hearing on reasonableness of the 100 per cent success fee.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appeal raises important practice points on the interrelation of Costs Practice Direction paragraphs 11.7 and 11.8(2), the court may allow the appeal to proceed despite new arguments but impose conditions under CPR 52.9(1) and order a re-hearing so the reasonableness of the original success fee can be examined.
legal_issues: Whether raising a new success fee argument on appeal was an abuse of process
How paragraphs 11.7 and 11.8(2) of the Costs Practice Direction interact
Whether the appropriate success fee should be assessed at CFA inception or later stages
Whether a re-hearing was necessary to determine reasonableness of the 100 per cent fee

notes: Restrictive covenant trial on equity derivatives broker; Cox J's construction and severance analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: TFS Derivatives v Morgan: enforceability of broker non-compete covenant
key_facts: Equity derivatives broker Simon Morgan resigned from TFS to join competitor GFI and was placed on three months' garden leave.
Clause 12.1(a) of his contract restrained competition in the relevant business activity for six months after employment, reduced by any garden leave period.
TFS sought to enforce the covenant after experience with another broker whose non-solicitation undertakings proved unpoliceable.
Morgan abandoned his repudiatory breach argument at trial and defended only on unreasonable restraint of trade grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited Queen's Bench trial of injunctive enforcement of post-termination restrictive covenants after interim undertakings.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction granted enforcing clause 12.1(a) with the words 'or similar to' severed; clauses 12.1(b) and (c) upheld but no injunction granted for lack of breach evidence.
enrichment.ratio: A non-compete clause in a broker's contract refers to the business activity in which the employee was materially involved, not employment by a competing entity in any capacity; where 'or similar to' extends the restraint beyond competitive activity without justification it may be severed, and a short post-termination non-compete may reasonably protect client connection and confidential brokerage information where non-solicitation covenants are ineffective.
legal_issues: Whether clause 12.1(a) prohibited working for GFI in any capacity or only in the relevant business activity
Whether garden leave for six months would be a more reasonable alternative to a non-compete
Whether the words 'or similar to' rendered the covenant unreasonably wide
Whether injunctive relief was appropriate for non-enticement covenants absent evidence of breach
linked_authorities: Office Angels Ltd v Rainer-Thomas and O'Connor [1991] IRLR 214
Arbuthnot Fund Managers Ltd v Rawlings [2003] EWCA Civ 518
Printers and Finishers Ltd v Holloway [1965] 1 WLR 1

notes: Green Belt cemetery planning appeal JR; Keith J's PPG2 and PPG17 analysis is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Kemnal Manor: Green Belt cemetery and crematorium planning appeal challenge
key_facts: The developer appealed against refusal of hybrid planning permission for a cemetery and crematorium on Green Belt land including former playing fields at Flamingo Park.
An inspector dismissed the appeal finding inappropriate Green Belt development with no very special circumstances and loss of playing fields not justified under PPG17.
The developer conceded inappropriateness before the inspector and focused on very special circumstances including local burial need.
Independent assessment showed surplus playing pitches locally but did not address wider open space uses or demonstrate community support.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court section 288 challenge to an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the inspector's conclusions on Green Belt inappropriateness, very special circumstances and playing fields were not legally flawed.
enrichment.ratio: A crematorium-dominated scheme may be inappropriate Green Belt development where intensity of use, access works and a chimneystack reduce openness; under PPG17 paragraph 10 an assessment must address alternative open space uses and developers should demonstrate wide community support, though absence of support is not determinative of lawfulness.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in treating the whole scheme as inappropriate Green Belt development
Whether very special circumstances including burial need were given insufficient weight
Whether the playing fields assessment under PPG17 paragraphs 10 and 15 was adequate
Whether requiring wide community support under PPG17 paragraph 10 was unlawful
linked_authorities: Pehrsson v Secretary of State for the Environment (1990) 61 P&CR 266
R (Newsmith Stainless Ltd) v Secretary of State for Environment, Transport and the Regions [2001] EWHC 74 (Admin)

notes: Brief permission decision on late witness statement costs; discretionary reasoning is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Newman v Adlem: permission to appeal costs of late witness statement application
key_facts: The claimant company sought permission to serve witness statements out of time about five weeks before trial.
The deputy judge admitted the evidence as disproportionate to refuse and ordered the defendant to pay the claimant's costs of the application.
The defendant opposed admission but did not consent, causing the costs of the formal application.
The sum in dispute was about £400.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal a deputy Chancery judge's costs order on a late witness statement application.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; no reasonable prospect of success on appeal against the costs order.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant requires a formal contested application to admit late witness statements rather than consenting, it is within the judge's costs discretion to order the defendant to pay the costs of that application even though the claimant was late in serving the statements.
legal_issues: Whether the party who was late with evidence should necessarily pay the costs of the permission application
Whether a formalistic approach to CPR costs rules should prevail over discretion
Whether the defendant's opposition rather than consent caused the application costs

notes: Defamation costs assessment delay after 1996 trial; Eady J's CPR 47.8 analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Botham v Niazi: delay in commencing defamation costs detailed assessment
key_facts: Botham and Lamb's 1996 defamation actions against Imran Khan ended with costs orders including separate costs of a withdrawn justification plea.
The parties agreed extensions to commence taxation and negotiate, but detailed assessment was not commenced until October 2003, over seven years later.
The claimants applied to stay or strike out assessment or disallow costs for delay and defective certification.
Both sides had contributed to delay and the claimants had not preserved their former solicitors' files.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in outstanding defamation detailed assessment proceedings to prevent continuation after long delay.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; assessment may continue though disallowance of interest was already conceded and full disallowance would be disproportionate.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to commence detailed assessment within three months engages CPR 47.8 but, where the paying party agreed extensions to negotiate and also delayed, total disallowance under rule 44.14 for misconduct is disproportionate; a bill certified not to exceed the amount actually paid to former solicitors can comply with the indemnity principle even if line items exceed that sum.
legal_issues: Whether seven-year delay warranted disallowing all of the defendant's assessed costs
Whether agreed extensions waived the breach of rule 47.7
Whether loss of solicitors' files caused irremediable prejudice
Whether the defendant's bill was invalid for defective certification under the Costs Practice Direction
linked_authorities: McGuigan v Tarmac Ltd (Current Law Year Book 2003 para 324)
Re Homes Assured: Sampson v Wilson [2002] 1 Costs LR 71
Biguzzi v Rank Leisure plc [1999] 1 WLR 1926

notes: Ancillary relief consent order appeal; section 24A jurisdiction and bankruptcy analysis is authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Ram v Ram: consent ancillary relief order, bankruptcy and section 24A jurisdiction
key_facts: After solicitors exchanged open letters accepting four core consent terms, Hedley J made an order with penal notice requiring immediate transfer of the matrimonial home and sale of 11 Westfield Road.
The husband was an undischarged bankrupt and his interest in Westfield Road was vested in his trustee; the wife had no interest in that property.
The order included enforcement provisions and maintenance pending suit contrary to the agreed clean-break terms.
The husband had not been given a fair opportunity to be heard on enforcement before the penal order was sealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against a consent ancillary relief order made after accepted without-prejudice negotiations.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and appeal allowed in part; order reduced to core consent terms with enforcement and section 24A sale provisions struck out; related applications by the husband's brothers partially allowed.
enrichment.ratio: A consent ancillary relief order may not incorporate rigid enforcement machinery with a penal notice without giving the party an opportunity to be heard; section 24A(1) requires a beneficial interest in possession or reversion and a bankrupt has no such interest in assets vested in the trustee until a surplus is finally ascertained following Ayerst v C&K Construction.
legal_issues: Whether the judge impermissibly converted consent order drafting into immediate enforcement
Whether section 24A(1) permitted an order for sale of property vested in a trustee in bankruptcy
Whether the husband retained a reversionary interest in bankruptcy assets
Whether section 24A(6) procedural requirements were satisfied for non-party brothers
linked_authorities: Ayerst (Inspector of Taxes) v C & K (Construction) Ltd [1976] AC 167
Ram v Ram [2003] EWCA Civ 243
Hadkinson v Hadkinson [1952] P 285

notes: Council tax liability order JR on service; Mitting J's analysis of magistrates' inherent jurisdiction is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Tull v Camberwell Green: council tax liability orders and defective service
key_facts: Mrs Tull owned a house split into flats but was not the occupier of Flat 1; tenant Miss Verma was the council tax payer until she left.
Lambeth issued liability orders in 1996 and 1998 after serving summonses at the tenanted flat as Mrs Tull's last known place of abode.
The council's records and electoral register information showed the flat was not her place of abode and managing agents later confirmed the tenant had vacated.
Magistrates refused to set aside the orders despite the council later accepting liability only for vacant periods.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of magistrates' liability orders and refusal to set them aside for defective service.
enrichment.outcome: Three liability orders quashed; council joined as defendant and ordered to pay 50% of assessed costs plus prior wasted costs order.
enrichment.ratio: Under regulation 35(2)(c) 'last known place of abode' means last place known to the billing authority after reasonable enquiry, not merely an address on the property; liability orders founded on invalid service may be set aside using magistrates' inherent jurisdiction where a substantial procedural error occurred and the defendant promptly applied on learning of the orders.
legal_issues: Whether service at a tenanted flat was service at the owner's last known place of abode
Whether the council took reasonable steps to ascertain Mrs Tull's abode
Whether magistrates had power to set aside liability orders for procedural error
Whether the claim was academic where the council accepted limited liability
linked_authorities: Liverpool City Council v Pleroma Distribution Ltd [2002] EWHC 2467 (Admin)
R (Brighton & Hove City Council) v Brighton & Hove Justices [2004] EWHC Admin
Mersey Docks Property Holdings v Kilgour [2004] EWHC 1638 (TCC)

notes: Wasted costs application over academic immigration JR; three-stage test applied and dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Latchman: wasted costs application over academic immigration judicial review
key_facts: Mrs Latchman obtained an out-of-hours injunction preventing removal so she could complete exams after removal directions were cancelled.
She continued judicial review after exams ended even though removal directions were no longer extant and voluntary departure remained possible.
The Secretary of State warned the solicitors the claim was an abuse and might attract a wasted costs order.
Solicitors struggled to contact the client in September 2004 before withdrawing the claim on 8 October 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court wasted costs application against the claimant's solicitors after withdrawal of an immigration judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Wasted costs application dismissed; judicial review dismissed and Gage J's interim order discharged; no order as to costs save detailed assessment of legal aid costs.
enrichment.ratio: A wasted costs order requires improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct causing unnecessary costs; solicitors who repeatedly tried to contact an unresponsive client before withdrawing an academic claim did not act unreasonably even if they failed to keep the Treasury Solicitor informed of those difficulties.
legal_issues: Whether pursuing the JR after 1 August 2004 was unreasonable or vexatious
Whether solicitors acted unreasonably in delaying withdrawal until October
Whether an outstanding Article 3 complaint kept the claim alive
Whether the three-stage wasted costs test under CPR was satisfied
linked_authorities: Medcalf v Mardell [2002] UKHL 27
Ridehalgh v Horsefield [1994] Ch 205
